desc:
There are n towers at positions points[i] = [x, y]. Building a cable between towers i and j costs min(|xi - xj|, |yi - yj|): only the smaller of the two coordinate differences counts.

Return the minimum total cost of cables needed so that every tower is connected to every other tower, directly or through other towers.

points = [[0,0],[3,1],[7,2]]   -> 2
(0-1 costs min(3,1) = 1, 1-2 costs min(4,1) = 1, 0-2 costs min(7,2) = 2)
hints: Taking every pair gives about n²/2 candidate cables, which is too many for n = 4,000 in the worst case. You need a much smaller candidate set that still contains an MST.

Sort the towers by x. For a cable between towers that are not neighbours in this order, there is a tower in between with both x-differences smaller. What does that say about the cost of the cables that go through it?
Only neighbours in the x-sorted order and neighbours in the y-sorted order need to be considered: that is at most 2(n - 1) cables. Run Kruskal on them.
editorial: Consider a cable between towers i and j with cost c = min(dx, dy), and suppose c = dx (the case c = dy is symmetric with the y-order). If another tower k lies between i and j in the x-order, then both |xi - xk| and |xk - xj| are at most dx, so the cables i-k and k-j each cost at most c. The cable i-j is then a heaviest edge of the cycle i-k-j, and by the cycle property it is not needed in some minimum spanning tree.

Therefore an MST exists that uses only cables between towers that are neighbours in the x-sorted order or neighbours in the y-sorted order. That is at most 2(n - 1) cables. Sort them by cost and run Kruskal with union-find: O(n log n) in total, in contrast to O(n² log n) for the complete graph.
